claim: Alcohol consumption in pregnancy is a leading cause of neurodevelopmental impairments in children.
source: Alcohol consumption in pregnancy is a leading cause of neurodevelopmental impairments in children (Popova et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Popova et al., 2023

claim: Alcohol can pass through the placenta acting as a teratogen in fetal tissues causing physical, cognitive, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental impairment in children at high doses with lifelong consequences for health.
source: Alcohol can pass through the placenta acting as a teratogen in fetal tissues causing physical, cognitive, behavioural, and neurodevelopmental impairment in children at high doses with lifelong consequences for health (Chung et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2021

claim: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) and fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) can arise at binge levels of exposure, although not always at lower levels of exposure.
source: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) and fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) can arise at binge levels of exposure, although not always at lower levels of exposure.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about FASD and FAS

claim: Whether prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) is sufficient to induce overt physiological abnormalities depends on multiple environmental and genetic factors including the dose and timing of alcohol use during pregnancy, maternal diet, smoking, stress, and potentially other factors that collectively influence fetal outcomes.
source: Whether prenatal alcohol exposure (PAE) is sufficient to induce overt physiological abnormalities depends on multiple environmental and genetic factors including the dose and timing of alcohol use during pregnancy, maternal diet, smoking, stress, and potentially other factors that collectively influence fetal outcomes (Chung et al., 2021; Jacobson et al., 2021; Sambo and Goldman, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chung et al., 2021; Jacobson et al., 2021; Sambo and Goldman, 2023

claim: Most women in Western countries consume low to moderate levels of alcohol between conception until recognition of pregnancy.
source: Patterns of alcohol consumption in pregnancy vary, but epidemiological surveys suggest most women in Western countries consume low to moderate levels between conception until recognition of pregnancy (Tsang et al., 2022), after which time consumption largely ceases, apart from occasional use (McCormack et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to epidemiological surveys (Tsang et al., 2022; McCormack et al., 2017)

claim: Alcohol consumption largely ceases after pregnancy recognition, apart from occasional use.
source: Patterns of alcohol consumption in pregnancy vary, but epidemiological surveys suggest most women in Western countries consume low to moderate levels between conception until recognition of pregnancy (Tsang et al., 2022), after which time consumption largely ceases, apart from occasional use (McCormack et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCormack et al., 2017

claim: The effects of binge levels of alcohol exposure are well documented as able to cause FASD.
source: While the effects of binge levels of exposure are well documented as able to cause FASD, more subtle effects that reflect the more common patterns of drinking are unclear and more research is needed to support public health initiatives to reduce alcohol consumption in pregnancy.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about binge drinking and FASD

claim: More subtle effects of alcohol that reflect the more common patterns of drinking are unclear and more research is needed.
source: While the effects of binge levels of exposure are well documented as able to cause FASD, more subtle effects that reflect the more common patterns of drinking are unclear and more research is needed to support public health initiatives to reduce alcohol consumption in pregnancy.
evidence: Inference from the state of the literature

claim: Alcohol can disrupt fetal gene regulation through epigenetic mechanisms.
source: Studies suggest alcohol can disrupt fetal gene regulation through epigenetic mechanisms (Bestry et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bestry et al., 2022

claim: DNA methylation involves the catalytic addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases within cytosine-guanine (CpG) dinucleotide motifs during one-carbon metabolism.
source: DNA methylation is one epigenetic mechanism involving the catalytic addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases within cytosine-guanine (CpG) dinucleotide motifs during one-carbon metabolism.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about DNA methylation

claim: Methylation of DNA can alter chromatin density and influence patterns of gene expression in a tissue-specific and developmentally appropriate manner.
source: Methylation of DNA can alter chromatin density and influence patterns of gene expression in a tissue-specific and developmentally appropriate manner and disruption to this process may cause some of the difficulties experienced by people with FASD (Jin and Liu, 2018; Fransquet et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin and Liu, 2018; Fransquet et al., 2016

claim: Disruption to DNA methylation may cause some of the difficulties experienced by people with FASD.
source: Methylation of DNA can alter chromatin density and influence patterns of gene expression in a tissue-specific and developmentally appropriate manner and disruption to this process may cause some of the difficulties experienced by people with FASD (Jin and Liu, 2018; Fransquet et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jin and Liu, 2018; Fransquet et al., 2016

claim: Previous studies on human participants report that alcohol can disrupt DNA methylation either globally or at specific gene regions.
source: Previous studies on human participants (Lussier et al., 2018; Masemola et al., 2015; Jarmasz et al., 2019; Portales-Casamar et al., 2016) and animals (Chen et al., 2013; Abbott et al., 2018; Downing et al., 2011) report that alcohol can disrupt DNA methylation either globally (Jarmasz et al., 2019; Portales-Casamar et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2013; Abbott et al., 2018) or at specific gene regions (Masemola et al., 2015; Abbott et al., 2018; Downing et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to human and animal studies

claim: Previous studies on animals report that alcohol can disrupt DNA methylation either globally or at specific gene regions.
source: Previous studies on human participants (Lussier et al., 2018; Masemola et al., 2015; Jarmasz et al., 2019; Portales-Casamar et al., 2016) and animals (Chen et al., 2013; Abbott et al., 2018; Downing et al., 2011) report that alcohol can disrupt DNA methylation either globally (Jarmasz et al., 2019; Portales-Casamar et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2013; Abbott et al., 2018) or at specific gene regions (Masemola et al., 2015; Abbott et al., 2018; Downing et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to animal studies

claim: A systematic review found limited replication of alcohol effects on DNA methylation between studies suggesting the effects may be stochastic and influenced by numerous confounding factors.
source: Our recent systematic review, however, found limited replication of effects between studies suggesting the effects of alcohol on DNA methylation may be stochastic and influenced by numerous confounding factors (Bestry et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bestry et al., 2022 systematic review

claim: PAE can directly inhibit DNA methyltransferase enzymes.
source: PAE can either directly inhibit DNA methyltransferase enzymes or disrupt one-carbon metabolism via inhibition of bioavailability of dietary methyl donors, such as folate and choline to the fetus (Chen et al., 2011; Hutson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2011; Hutson et al., 2012

claim: PAE can disrupt one-carbon metabolism via inhibition of bioavailability of dietary methyl donors, such as folate and choline to the fetus.
source: PAE can either directly inhibit DNA methyltransferase enzymes or disrupt one-carbon metabolism via inhibition of bioavailability of dietary methyl donors, such as folate and choline to the fetus (Chen et al., 2011; Hutson et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2011; Hutson et al., 2012

claim: Choline has been explored in several clinical trials to reduce cognitive deficits caused by PAE in affected individuals.
source: Choline, in particular, has been explored in several clinical trials to reduce cognitive deficits caused by PAE in affected individuals (Nguyen et al., 2016; Wozniak et al., 2020), or when administered during pregnancy (Jacobson et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2009), with results suggesting a high methyl donor (HMD) diet could at least partially mitigate the adverse effects of PAE on various behavioural outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical trials (Nguyen et al., 2016; Wozniak et al., 2020; Jacobson et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2009)

claim: A high methyl donor (HMD) diet could at least partially mitigate the adverse effects of PAE on various behavioural outcomes.
source: Choline, in particular, has been explored in several clinical trials to reduce cognitive deficits caused by PAE in affected individuals (Nguyen et al., 2016; Wozniak et al., 2020), or when administered during pregnancy (Jacobson et al., 2018; Thomas et al., 2009), with results suggesting a high methyl donor (HMD) diet could at least partially mitigate the adverse effects of PAE on various behavioural outcomes.
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical trials suggesting this effect

claim: The exposure period in the murine model covers the equivalent of pre-conception up until the first trimester in humans when neurulation occurs.
source: The exposure period covers the equivalent of pre-conception up until the first trimester in humans when neurulation occurs, reflecting a typical situation in which women may consume alcohol up until pregnancy recognition (Tsang et al., 2022; Muggli et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on comparison of murine and human developmental timelines

claim: The murine exposure period reflects a typical situation in which women may consume alcohol up until pregnancy recognition.
source: The exposure period covers the equivalent of pre-conception up until the first trimester in humans when neurulation occurs, reflecting a typical situation in which women may consume alcohol up until pregnancy recognition (Tsang et al., 2022; Muggli et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tsang et al., 2022; Muggli et al., 2016

claim: Brain and liver are two target organs affected by ethanol.
source: We employed whole-genome bisulfite sequencing (WGBS) for unbiased assessment of CpG DNA methylation in newborn brain and liver, two target organs affected by ethanol (Zakhari, 2006), to explore tissue specificity of effects and to determine any 'tissue agnostic' effects which may have arisen prior to the germ layers separating in early gastrulation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Zakhari, 2006

claim: Common patterns of drinking can have measurable effects on fetal gene regulation.
source: Our study provides cogent evidence that common patterns of drinking can have measurable effects on fetal gene regulation, highlighting a role for maternal dietary support in public health interventions.
evidence: Based on the experimental data presented in the study

claim: There is a role for maternal dietary support in public health interventions related to alcohol consumption in pregnancy.
source: Our study provides cogent evidence that common patterns of drinking can have measurable effects on fetal gene regulation, highlighting a role for maternal dietary support in public health interventions.
evidence: Inferred from the study findings on HMD diet effects

claim: The trajectory of weight gain during pregnancy was similar across all treatment groups.
source: The trajectory of weight gain during pregnancy was similar across all treatment groups with some evidence of more rapid weight gain in the HMD groups in the last 2 days (linear mixed effects regression model; H2O-HMD: –2.282±0.918 g, p=0.0177; PAE-HMD: –1.656±0.814 g, p=0.0493; Figure 2a), although the total amount of weight gained between days 1 and 17–19 was not significantly different between treatment groups by linear mixed effects regression (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2a and b

claim: HMD groups showed more rapid weight gain in the last 2 days of pregnancy.
source: The trajectory of weight gain during pregnancy was similar across all treatment groups with some evidence of more rapid weight gain in the HMD groups in the last 2 days (linear mixed effects regression model; H2O-HMD: –2.282±0.918 g, p=0.0177; PAE-HMD: –1.656±0.814 g, p=0.0493; Figure 2a), although the total amount of weight gained between days 1 and 17–19 was not significantly different between treatment groups by linear mixed effects regression (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p=0.0177 for H2O-HMD; p=0.0493 for PAE-HMD) and Figure 2a

claim: The total amount of weight gained between days 1 and 17–19 was not significantly different between treatment groups.
source: The trajectory of weight gain during pregnancy was similar across all treatment groups with some evidence of more rapid weight gain in the HMD groups in the last 2 days (linear mixed effects regression model; H2O-HMD: –2.282±0.918 g, p=0.0177; PAE-HMD: –1.656±0.814 g, p=0.0493; Figure 2a), although the total amount of weight gained between days 1 and 17–19 was not significantly different between treatment groups by linear mixed effects regression (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis and Figure 2a and b

claim: The total amount of liquid consumed over the course of pregnancy was significantly lower in HMD dams.
source: The total amount of liquid consumed over the course of pregnancy was significantly lower in HMD dams by unpaired t-test (Figure 2b and Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by unpaired t-test and Figures 2b and 3c

claim: There was no significant difference in the average litter size between treatment groups.
source: There was no significant difference in the average litter size (6.525±0.297 pups, Figure 2c) and pup sex ratios (Figure 2d) between treatment groups by unpaired t-test.
evidence: Supported by unpaired t-test and Figure 2c

claim: The average litter size was 6.525±0.297 pups.
source: There was no significant difference in the average litter size (6.525±0.297 pups, Figure 2c) and pup sex ratios (Figure 2d) between treatment groups by unpaired t-test.
evidence: Supported by experimental data and Figure 2c

claim: There was no significant difference in pup sex ratios between treatment groups.
source: There was no significant difference in the average litter size (6.525±0.297 pups, Figure 2c) and pup sex ratios (Figure 2d) between treatment groups by unpaired t-test.
evidence: Supported by unpaired t-test and Figure 2d

claim: A total of 21,842,961 CpG sites were initially available for analysis.
source: A total of 21,842,961 CpG sites were initially available for analysis.
evidence: Reported from the WGBS data

claim: Global levels of DNA methylation stratified across different genomic contexts were preserved across treatment conditions, with no major differences in average DNA methylation content between groups.
source: Global levels of DNA methylation stratified across different genomic contexts were preserved across treatment conditions, with no major differences in average DNA methylation content between groups (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4

claim: 78 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) were identified in the brain comparing exposed and unexposed mice on normal chow.
source: We identified 78 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) in the brain and 759 DMRs in the liver (p<0.05 and mean difference in methylation across the DMR with PAE (delta) >0.05) from ~19,000,000 CpG sites tested after coverage filtering (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Supported by genome-wide testing and Figure 5a

claim: 759 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) were identified in the liver comparing exposed and unexposed mice on normal chow.
source: We identified 78 differentially methylated regions (DMRs) in the brain and 759 DMRs in the liver (p<0.05 and mean difference in methylation across the DMR with PAE (delta) >0.05) from ~19,000,000 CpG sites tested after coverage filtering (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: Supported by genome-wide testing and Figure 5b

claim: Two of the DMRs overlapped in mouse brain and liver (tissue agnostic), but the remainder were tissue specific.
source: Two of the DMRs overlapped in mouse brain and liver (tissue agnostic), but the remainder were tissue specific.
evidence: Supported by analysis of DMR overlap between tissues

claim: The Impact gene on chromosome 18 had lower methylation in PAE+NC mice compared to H2O+NC mice in both the brain and liver.
source: Among these tissue agnostic regions was the Impact gene on chromosome 18, which had lower methylation in PAE+NC mice compared to H2O+NC mice in both the brain and liver (Figure 5c and d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5c and d

claim: A region within 5 kb downstream of Bmf had higher DNA methylation in brain and liver tissue of PAE+NC mice.
source: The other tissue agnostic region was within 5 kb downstream of Bmf and had higher DNA methylation in brain and liver tissue of PAE+NC mice.
evidence: Supported by DMR analysis data

claim: Lower DNA methylation with early moderate PAE in NC mice was more frequently observed in liver DMRs (93.5% of liver DMRs).
source: Lower DNA methylation with early moderate PAE in NC mice was more frequently observed in liver DMRs (93.5% of liver DMRs), while brain DMRs were almost equally divided between lower and higher DNA methylation with early moderate PAE (52.6% of brain DMRs had lower DNA methylation with early moderate PAE).
evidence: Supported by analysis of DMR directionality

claim: 52.6% of brain DMRs had lower DNA methylation with early moderate PAE.
source: Lower DNA methylation with early moderate PAE in NC mice was more frequently observed in liver DMRs (93.5% of liver DMRs), while brain DMRs were almost equally divided between lower and higher DNA methylation with early moderate PAE (52.6% of brain DMRs had lower DNA methylation with early moderate PAE).
evidence: Supported by analysis of DMR directionality

claim: The three genes affected by PAE in both brain and the liver tissues were the Autism Susceptibility Gene 2 (Auts2), Androglobin (Adgb), and RNA Binding Protein Fox 1 (Rbfox1) genes.
source: The three genes affected by PAE in both brain and the liver tissues were the Autism Susceptibility Gene 2 (Auts2), Androglobin (Adgb), and RNA Binding Protein Fox 1 (Rbfox1) genes (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data in Table 1

claim: In both brain and liver tissues, DMRs were enriched in non-coding intergenic and open sea regions and relatively underrepresented in coding and CpG island regions.
source: In both brain and liver tissues, DMRs were enriched in non-coding intergenic and open sea regions and relatively underrepresented in coding and CpG island regions (Figure 5e and f).
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5e and f

claim: DMRs were enriched in open chromatin regions (ATAC-seq), enhancer regions (H3K4me1), and active gene promoter regions (H3K27ac), in mouse fetal forebrain tissue and fetal liver.
source: Using open chromatin assay and histone modification datasets from the ENCODE project, we found enrichment (p<0.05) of DMRs in open chromatin regions (ATAC-seq), enhancer regions (H3K4me1), and active gene promoter regions (H3K27ac), in mouse fetal forebrain tissue and fetal liver (Table 2).
evidence: Supported by ENCODE data analysis with p<0.05 and Table 2

claim: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of liver DMRs showed enrichment in 10 predominantly neuronal pathways, with neuron projection being the most significant.
source: Gene ontology enrichment analysis of liver DMRs that did localise to genes showed enrichment in 10 predominantly neuronal pathways, with neuron projection being the most significant (Figure 5g, Supplementary file 1c and d).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 5g and supplementary files

claim: PAE+HMD mice exhibited significant DNA methylation differences in only 12/78 (15%) brain DMRs compared to control mice.
source: Compared to control mice (H2O+NC), PAE+HMD mice exhibited significant (p<0.05) DNA methylation differences in only 12/78 (15%) brain (Supplementary file 1g), and 124/759 (16%) liver (Supplementary file 1h) DMRs, suggesting the effects were predominantly mitigated.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p<0.05) and supplementary file 1g

claim: PAE+HMD mice exhibited significant DNA methylation differences in only 124/759 (16%) liver DMRs compared to control mice.
source: Compared to control mice (H2O+NC), PAE+HMD mice exhibited significant (p<0.05) DNA methylation differences in only 12/78 (15%) brain (Supplementary file 1g), and 124/759 (16%) liver (Supplementary file 1h) DMRs, suggesting the effects were predominantly mitigated.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis (p<0.05) and supplementary file 1h

claim: The effects of PAE on DNA methylation were predominantly mitigated by HMD.
source: Compared to control mice (H2O+NC), PAE+HMD mice exhibited significant (p<0.05) DNA methylation differences in only 12/78 (15%) brain (Supplementary file 1g), and 124/759 (16%) liver (Supplementary file 1h) DMRs, suggesting the effects were predominantly mitigated.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction in significant DMRs in HMD mice

claim: Effect sizes compared to mice on the normal chow were substantially lower in mice on the HMD diet, in some cases more than 25% reduced.
source: Effect sizes compared to mice on the normal chow were substantially lower, in some cases more than 25% reduced in mice on the HMD diet (Figure 6).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6

claim: There was no evidence that early moderate PAE had a significant effect on any of the behavioural outcomes tested.
source: There was no evidence that early moderate PAE had a significant effect on any of the behavioural outcomes tested (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by behavioural testing data shown in Figure 7

claim: Mice exposed to HMD exhibited greater locomotor activity, in terms of distance travelled.
source: Mice exposed to HMD exhibited greater locomotor activity, in terms of distance travelled (Figure 8).
evidence: Supported by behavioural testing data shown in Figure 8

claim: Only 36 of the 78 (46.2%) brain DMRs had homologous regions in the human genome that were able to be tested.
source: Only 36 of the 78 (46.2%) brain DMRs, and 294 of the 759 (38.8%) liver DMRs, had homologous regions in the human genome that were able to be tested.
evidence: Supported by liftover analysis results

claim: Only 294 of the 759 (38.8%) liver DMRs had homologous regions in the human genome that were able to be tested.
source: Only 36 of the 78 (46.2%) brain DMRs, and 294 of the 759 (38.8%) liver DMRs, had homologous regions in the human genome that were able to be tested.
evidence: Supported by liftover analysis results

claim: No evidence of differential DNA methylation was found at CpG sites corresponding to mouse DMRs in the AQUA cohort comparing 'never exposed' newborns to 'any exposure'.
source: We performed differential testing on a total of 1898 CpG sites that corresponded to mouse DMRs, comparing 'never exposed' newborns to 'any exposure' and found no evidence of differential DNA methylation at these CpG (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by differential testing in the AQUA cohort

claim: Seven DMR associations with FASD status were statistically replicated in the Canadian clinical cohort after adjusting for participant age, sex, array number, and estimated cell counts.
source: Differential testing of a total of 2316 CpG sites that were homologous to mouse DMRs statistically replicated seven DMR associations with FASD status (FDR p<0.05) after adjusting for participant age, sex, array number, and estimated cell counts (Table 3).
evidence: Supported by differential testing with FDR p<0.05 and Table 3

claim: Genes associated with the seven replicated DMRs are linked to clinically relevant traits including facial morphology, educational attainment, intelligence, autism and schizophrenia.
source: Genes associated with these DMRs are linked to clinically relevant traits in the GWAS catalogue including facial morphology (GADD45A; Indencleef et al., 2021), educational attainment (AP2B1; Okbay et al., 2022), intelligence (RP9; Davies et al., 2019), autism and schizophrenia (ZNF823; Autism Spectrum Disorders Working Group of The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to GWAS studies

claim: GADD45A is linked to facial morphology.
source: Genes associated with these DMRs are linked to clinically relevant traits in the GWAS catalogue including facial morphology (GADD45A; Indencleef et al., 2021), educational attainment (AP2B1; Okbay et al., 2022), intelligence (RP9; Davies et al., 2019), autism and schizophrenia (ZNF823; Autism Spectrum Disorders Working Group of The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Indencleef et al., 2021

claim: AP2B1 is linked to educational attainment.
source: Genes associated with these DMRs are linked to clinically relevant traits in the GWAS catalogue including facial morphology (GADD45A; Indencleef et al., 2021), educational attainment (AP2B1; Okbay et al., 2022), intelligence (RP9; Davies et al., 2019), autism and schizophrenia (ZNF823; Autism Spectrum Disorders Working Group of The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Okbay et al., 2022

claim: RP9 is linked to intelligence.
source: Genes associated with these DMRs are linked to clinically relevant traits in the GWAS catalogue including facial morphology (GADD45A; Indencleef et al., 2021), educational attainment (AP2B1; Okbay et al., 2022), intelligence (RP9; Davies et al., 2019), autism and schizophrenia (ZNF823; Autism Spectrum Disorders Working Group of The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Davies et al., 2019

claim: ZNF823 is linked to autism and schizophrenia.
source: Genes associated with these DMRs are linked to clinically relevant traits in the GWAS catalogue including facial morphology (GADD45A; Indencleef et al., 2021), educational attainment (AP2B1; Okbay et al., 2022), intelligence (RP9; Davies et al., 2019), autism and schizophrenia (ZNF823; Autism Spectrum Disorders Working Group of The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Autism Spectrum Disorders Working Group of The Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2017

claim: Moderate early prenatal alcohol exposure was sufficient to affect site-specific DNA methylation in newborn pups without altering behavioural outcomes in adult littermates.
source: Early moderate PAE was sufficient to affect site-specific DNA methylation in newborn pups without altering behavioural outcomes in adult littermates.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from WGBS and behavioural testing

claim: DNA methylation differences were enriched in non-coding genomic regions with regulatory potential indicative of broad effects of alcohol on genome regulation.
source: DNA methylation differences were enriched in non-coding genomic regions with regulatory potential indicative of broad effects of alcohol on genome regulation.
evidence: Supported by enrichment analysis of DMRs

claim: Some DNA methylation effects of PAE were metastable at genes linked to disease-relevant traits including facial morphology, intelligence, educational attainment, autism, and schizophrenia.
source: Replication studies in human cohorts with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder suggested some effects were metastable at genes linked to disease-relevant traits including facial morphology, intelligence, educational attainment, autism, and schizophrenia.
evidence: Supported by replication studies in human FASD cohorts

claim: A maternal diet high in folate and choline protected against some of the damaging effects of early moderate PAE on DNA methylation.
source: In our murine model, a maternal diet high in folate and choline protected against some of the damaging effects of early moderate PAE on DNA methylation.
evidence: Supported by comparison of DMRs in HMD vs NC mice

claim: Early moderate exposure is sufficient to affect fetal genome regulation even in the absence of overt phenotypic changes.
source: Our studies demonstrate that early moderate exposure is sufficient to affect fetal genome regulation even in the absence of overt phenotypic changes and highlight a role for preventative maternal dietary interventions.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing DNA methylation changes without behavioural changes

claim: There is a role for preventative maternal dietary interventions in the context of prenatal alcohol exposure.
source: Our studies demonstrate that early moderate exposure is sufficient to affect fetal genome regulation even in the absence of overt phenotypic changes and highlight a role for preventative maternal dietary interventions.
evidence: Inferred from the protective effects of HMD diet

claim: Alcohol effects on DNA methylation were predominantly tissue-specific.
source: In our model, alcohol effects on DNA methylation were predominantly tissue-specific, with only two genomic regions and four genes that were similarly affected in both liver and brain.
evidence: Supported by comparison of DMRs between brain and liver

claim: Some perturbations to DNA methylation may have been established stochastically because of PAE to the early embryo and maintained in the differentiating tissue.
source: These perturbations may have been established stochastically because of PAE to the early embryo and maintained in the differentiating tissue.
evidence: Speculative inference from tissue-agnostic DMRs

claim: More perturbations to the epigenome were observable in liver tissue, which may reflect the liver's specific role in metabolic detoxification of alcohol.
source: Indeed, most of the observed effects were tissue-specific, with more perturbations to the epigenome observable in liver tissue, which may reflect the liver's specific role in metabolic detoxification of alcohol.
evidence: Speculative inference from the greater number of liver DMRs

claim: Cell-type composition differences between brain and liver might explain differential sensitivity to alcohol effects.
source: Alternatively, cell-type composition differences between brain and liver might explain differential sensitivity to alcohol effects.
evidence: Speculative alternative explanation for tissue differences

claim: DMRs were enriched in non-coding regions of the genome with regulatory potential, suggesting alcohol has broad effects on genome regulation.
source: Generally, DMRs were enriched in non-coding regions of the genome with regulatory potential, suggesting alcohol has broad effects on genome regulation.
evidence: Inferred from enrichment analysis of DMRs

claim: Some associations identified in the murine model of early moderate exposure were recapitulated in human subjects with FASD despite species and biosample differences.
source: It is remarkable that some associations identified in our murine model of early moderate exposure were recapitulated in human subjects with FASD despite species and biosample differences, suggesting that at least some DNA methylation changes are stable over time.
evidence: Supported by replication studies in human FASD cohorts

claim: At least some DNA methylation changes caused by PAE are stable over time.
source: It is remarkable that some associations identified in our murine model of early moderate exposure were recapitulated in human subjects with FASD despite species and biosample differences, suggesting that at least some DNA methylation changes are stable over time.
evidence: Inferred from replication of DMRs in human FASD cohorts

claim: The effect size for replicated regions were strikingly smaller in blood samples from subjects with FASD suggesting the dose and duration of exposure may need to exceed a high threshold to survive reprogramming in the blood.
source: Notably the effect size for replicated regions were strikingly smaller in blood samples from subjects with FASD suggesting the dose and duration of exposure may need to exceed a high threshold to survive reprogramming in the blood.
evidence: Speculative inference from comparison of effect sizes

claim: The dose and duration of exposure threshold may explain lack of reproducibility in the AQUA cohort.
source: We speculate this may explain lack of reproducibility in the AQUA cohort.
evidence: Speculative explanation for lack of replication

claim: The candidate gene analysis replicated previously published reports of decreased DNA methylation within Peg3 and KvDMR1 from South African children with FAS.
source: In the candidate gene analysis we replicated previously published reports of decreased DNA methylation within Peg3 and KvDMR1 from South African children with FAS (Masemola et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by candidate gene analysis and citation to Masemola et al., 2015

claim: Both Peg3 and KvDMR1 genes are methylated in a parent-of-origin specific manner, suggesting that alcohol may affect imprinting processes.
source: Both genes are methylated in a parent-of-origin specific manner, suggesting that alcohol may affect imprinting processes.
evidence: Inference from the nature of Peg3 and KvDMR1 as imprinted genes

claim: Previous rodent and human studies have identified DNA methylation differences with PAE in imprinted regions such as the Igf2/H19 locus.
source: Previous rodent and human studies have identified DNA methylation differences with PAE in imprinted regions such as the Igf2/H19 locus (Portales-Casamar et al., 2016; Downing et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2016), although results are not entirely consistent (Marjonen et al., 2018; Stouder et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Results on DNA methylation differences with PAE in imprinted regions are not entirely consistent across studies.
source: Previous rodent and human studies have identified DNA methylation differences with PAE in imprinted regions such as the Igf2/H19 locus (Portales-Casamar et al., 2016; Downing et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2016), although results are not entirely consistent (Marjonen et al., 2018; Stouder et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations showing inconsistent results

claim: Duration of exposure, dose, and other tissue-related factors all likely influence the extent to which genome regulation is perturbed and manifests as differences in DNA methylation.
source: On the balance of this, we speculate duration of exposure, dose, and other tissue-related factors all likely influence the extent to which genome regulation is perturbed and manifests as differences in DNA methylation.
evidence: Speculative inference from the body of evidence

claim: The results are encouraging for biomarker studies and aid in the prioritisation of associations for future follow-up, particularly in relation to diagnosis of FASD.
source: Our results are encouraging for biomarker studies and aid in the prioritisation of associations for future follow-up, particularly in relation to diagnosis of FASD.

claim: Three genes that were validated in the Lussier et al., 2018 cohort are zinc finger proteins (RP9, PEX12, and ZNF823) that play an important role in fetal gene regulation.
